title: Teachers Jim Humphrey and Frank Welch; learning arranging
summary: Early neighbourhood musicians, lessons with Humphrey and Welch, learning to arrange and read, hearing his uncle and street bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Down in French, part of town. Around Perdita Street. I know you know those places. That's by Larry Armstrong. Yeah, Larry Armstrong. And Perdita and Rampard, different band. Bob Lyons and oh, I guess Frankie Deucin and all those guys. That was E-ball. Yeah, he played Trumbull. He was good. Very good. Tell me some more about your teachers. Oh, yeah. Now, a fellow that mostly, I got instruction from after my uncle died. I got from a fellow by the name of Jim Humphrey. Jim Humphrey. He had three or four sons. They're always musicians. Well, they're still living. And Willie, Willie, that's right. Yeah, uh-huh. Percy, a trumpet player. Yeah, that's right. I guess Earl Humphrey's dead. He's dead. He's been dead for years. 20 years. And there's one of them played clarinet. That was Willie. Willie. He's still playing. Yeah, yeah. And the old, old, old guy that his dad is named Willie too. I guess he's still playing Willie Humphrey. So I got good instruction from those fellows. And there was a fellow. Your teacher then is Willie? Jim Humphrey. Jim. Jim Humphrey. Yeah. And Frank Welch. Frank Welch was the man who taught me arranging and writing music. He wrote some of the most beautiful notes on a paper that you ever see. And I don't see how he could do it. He used to doctor with his ink, doctor his ink up with something that caused it to just stand right up. It wouldn't block, you know. And he taught me different phrases and how to keep out the other fellow's way, playing and playing a melody, you know, never get into the other fellow's melody. And he showed me how to, you know, keep in tone. He gave me instruction on the chords and how to form a chord, and what instrument could take the chord, and what instrument wouldn't take it, see. And he was a very good teacher. Very good. I had two, about two or three teachers that I went under. He was very good. Nice. There was kind, you know. There was kind fellows. And that way, if you've got a good, kind teacher, you can learn more, because he'll encourage, you see.
Mr. Welch, what was his first name?
What did he play? Any certain instrument better than others?
He played trumpet. He was a trumpet player. That's right. And a music arranger, beautiful music arranger.
When you started your very first lessons, did you learn to read music?
Your very first? Music that I started. Yeah. Did you start your music?

Yeah, he started me off in arranging and writing music, see. I heard my uncle play it several times, but I was too small to, you know, to take it up, see. But it seems like it stayed in my ear. Was that the first music you remember hearing, or the bands on the streets? Yeah, voice music, and then the bands on the street. That's the first music I began. Then I began to take an instrument, and after I learned scales and different things about the bands on the street, I began to learn, and then I played a little on violin and different instruments. And that's how I become familiar, more familiar with arranging than I did, see, because I was always mixed up with all the instruments. That's why when you hear me play trombone, I jump into somebody's part, but I sweeten it, see. That is make a nice melody to go in with that fellow that's playing. See, the average trombones, they play trombone, but they just play what they see, see. That is the music, they play just what they see. But if you know your chords and your phrases, you can play what you see, and then put more into it, see. In other words, improvise, see.
